title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) that tested whether a deterministic verifier pipeline (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered intent→configuration tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt-5-mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM call per task) producing model_calls_used = 200 (preregistered independent per‑arm generation would have used up to 400). Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0). Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that the deterministic verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this execution. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts, provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of testability failure, and give concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial injection calibration, and exploratory ROC reserves) for informative repeats.

sections.introduction: LLM-enabled intent→configuration translation promises to reduce operator effort in NetOps, but unsafe or misordered device changes can cause outages or security exposures. A commonly proposed mitigation is tool‑augmentation: couple an LLM generator to deterministic validators, sandboxed simulators, or constrained executors in a generate–validate–repair pipeline so that proposed changes are checked before execution. We preregistered a confirmatory paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) to quantify whether deterministic verifier augmentation causally reduces the frequency of verifier‑detected unsafe proposals from a hosted LLM under controlled benign and adversarial prompt clusters. The preregistered estimand was the paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded minus baseline), tested with an exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap CIs (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). The design sampled N=200 deterministically generated tasks and compared two pipelines under the two permitted generation semantics (independent per‑arm or shared_initial_candidate). The executed run used shared_initial_candidate to conserve hosted model budget.
sections.related_work: Surveys and prototype reports document rapid adoption of LLMs for NetOps tasks (intent translation, configuration synthesis, diagnosis and limited remediation) while calling attention to safety, verification, and evaluation gaps [1–3]. Prior technical work advocates tool‑augmentation (generate–validate–refine or divide–verify–refine) and reports improved adherence to constraints on curated tasks when an external verifier faithfully encodes the domain constraints; however, effect sizes and operational utility depend strongly on verifier fidelity, sampling semantics, and repair policies [4–6]. Studies of guardrails, schema‑based tool interfaces, and agent orchestration emphasize practical trade‑offs: stricter verification reduces obvious violations but can increase false refusals and operator burden unless ROC‑style diagnostics are measured and governance is tuned [2,7]. Our experiment aligns with these methodological prescriptions by (a) using a deterministic task generator and sandboxed deterministic validation, (b) preregistering a paired estimand with explicit exclusion and missingness rules, and (c) archiving full validator traces and execution/analysis manifests to enable deterministic replay and audit.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. The experiment was preregistered (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on binary SAFE indicators derived from deterministic sandbox validation. Confirmatory test: exact two‑sided McNemar (paired_binary_analysis_v1); CI method: paired bootstrap percentile (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Sampling and tasks. A deterministic task generator produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks (single‑AS, multi‑device topologies; allowed fields: admin, mtu, vlan). Tasks included explicit initial and expected final states and per‑task workflow policies. The preregistration reserved an exploratory calibration reserve (up to 50 tasks) for adversarial tuning prior to confirmatory execution. Pipelines compared. Baseline: accept the LLM candidate and post hoc score with deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Guarded: validate the same candidate in a deterministic sandbox; repair calls were permitted by the design but, for the executed confirmatory episodes, repair_provider_trace entries are null (no repairs applied). Generation semantics and budgeting. The preregistration allowed independent per‑arm draws (≈400 model calls) or shared_initial_candidate (one call per task). To fit the hosted budget the run executed shared_initial_candidate; model_calls_used = 200 (executed) versus maximum_model_calls = 400 (preregistered for independent draws). Scoring and analysis. The validator produced deterministic valid flags and structured violation lists. Binary SAFE = validator.valid (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE). Analysis computed the 2×2 contingency (n11,n10,n01,n00), exact McNemar p‑value, and paired bootstrap CI. Missingness and exclusion rules (one automatic retry per failed call; deterministic replacements for contaminated tasks) were applied as preregistered. Table 1 summarizes key resource trade‑offs (model_calls, N, generation semantics).
sections.results: Execution and reconciliation. The run completed 400 episodes (200 paired episodes) with zero technical failures and deterministic reconciliation checks passing. Provider audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and cache_miss_count = 200. Primary confirmatory outcomes. The deterministic validator labeled every confirmatory episode SAFE: baseline SAFE = 200/200 and guarded SAFE = 200/200. Contingency counts: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Representative validator traces for sampled tasks show validator.valid = true and violation_count = 0; repair traces are null, confirming that no repairs contributed to discordant outcomes. Missingness and contamination. The preregistered exploratory reserve was not consumed prior to confirmatory execution; missingness_summary shows complete_pairs = 200 and zero failed or unscorable episodes. Interpretation. These outcomes are artifact‑grounded and reproducible, but they make the preregistered causal contrast mechanically untestable under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics because both arms scored identical per‑pair candidates and no repairs or nondeterministic validator events produced discordance. The non‑informative ceiling result therefore reflects a combination of sampling semantics, observed baseline behavior, and budgeting choices rather than measured verifier efficacy.
sections.discussion: Root cause and diagnostic synthesis. The degenerate contingency arises from three archived facts: (1) shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM candidate per task shared across arms; (2) the deterministic validator labeled every candidate SAFE; and (3) no repairs were applied during confirmatory episodes. These three facts together precluded discordant pairs and rendered McNemar’s paired contrast uninformative. Consequences for confirmatory design. To test the causal effect of adding a verifier to generation, per‑arm independence (or an alternative mechanism that reliably produces guarded‑arm candidate changes, e.g., deterministic repairs) is required. Independent per‑arm draws would have required roughly 200 additional model calls for this N=200 design (preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400). Practical artifact‑grounded recommendations. Based on the archived run we recommend (a) budget independent per‑arm generation when the estimand is a paired causal contrast; (b) consume a preregistered exploratory reserve to calibrate adversarial transforms until baseline unsafe rates match power assumptions; (c) instrument and archive repair traces if repairs are permitted so that UNSAFE→SAFE conversions can be quantified; and (d) perform a small deterministic pilot before committing to the full confirmatory run and abort according to preregistered contingency‑preserving paths if pilot produces ceiling/floor outcomes. Alternative estimands. When budgets or policies preclude independent per‑arm draws, choose estimands compatible with shared semantics (absolute unsafe‑rate estimation, refusal/repair conversion rates, or ROC diagnostics using exploratory injections). Threats to validity and generality. The synthetic task family is limited (fields: admin/mtu/vlan; single‑AS topologies); validator completeness relative to real production failure modes is untested. The run evaluated a single declared model (gpt-5-mini). Operational implications. The run cannot quantify false‑refusal/operator burden trade‑offs because no refusals occurred; such measurement requires consuming the exploratory reserve and/or running repairs.
sections.conclusion: We performed a fully archived, preregistered paired experiment comparing gpt-5-mini baseline generation and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). Because identical per‑pair generations were used and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis was not testable in this run. The contribution is therefore methodological and reproducibility‑centred: (1) a complete deterministic preregistered run with archived artifacts permitting deterministic replay; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why this execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and (3) concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration, and exploratory ROC estimation) for informative repeats. Researchers seeking to repeat or extend this study should consult the archived bundle (preregistration, execution manifest, scoring traces and analysis artifacts) before changing preregistered design choices.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure Statement (CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track): Declared LLM: gpt-5-mini (execution recorded in the archived model configuration). Orchestration/framework: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter and deterministic experiment harness. Initial master prompt: archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt with immutable SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. Preregistration: cand-2026-01-prereg-v1 was frozen before execution and specified the estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), N=200 paired tasks, allowed generation semantics (independent per‑arm or shared_initial_candidate), scoring rules, and stopping rules. Executed generation semantics: independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate) so one shared LLM candidate per task was scored by both arms; model_calls_used = 200 while the preregistered independent per‑arm scenario would have used up to 400 model calls. Validator and scoring: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed deterministic sandboxed validation and emitted structured validation traces; confirmatory binary outcomes were derived from validator.valid (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE). Repairs: the pipeline design permitted one automatic repair call per task, but repair_provider_trace fields are null in all confirmatory scoring artifacts (no repairs applied). Analysis executor: paired_binary_analysis_v1 computed contingency counts, exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes were executed; the observed model call count reflects the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics. Reproducibility: full preregistration, execution manifests, scoring JSONs, validator traces and analysis artifacts are archived in the supplied bundle (consult the archived bundle for deterministic replay). Human editing: no manual human edits to technical content, analyses, or manuscript text occurred after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development: infrastructure rehearsals occurred prior to the autonomy lock and were excluded from final empirical evidence unless reproduced under the post‑lock execution.
limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt-5-mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
